title: How to Attain Single-Mindedness Without Distraction
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Question: How does one attain single-mindedness in Buddha-recitation?

inline.s: Question: How does one attain single-mindedness without distraction in Buddha-recitation?
Answer: This is a large topic, which I will answer below in five parts:

When the principle is clear, resolve is firm. You must investigate until you understand clearly: why should one recite the Buddha's name with single-mindedness without distraction? It is advisable to read carefully the Sutra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha's Reception, and deeply grasp why the World-Honored One taught mindful recollection without distraction (single-mindedness), and why he repeatedly urged us to “practice as taught.” (For reference, see
Commentary on the Sutra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha's Reception
Single-Mindedness Without Distraction
Answers on Single-Mindedness Without Distraction
) — and continue until you reach the point of full self-confidence and self-approval.

Question: In principle I know that recitation should achieve single-mindedness without distraction, but in practice I simply cannot arouse faith, and even think it is fundamentally unattainable, feeling deeply bewildered and oppressed. What should I do?

Answer: This shows that you lack the two stages of practice called “ceasing evil and practicing good” and “taking the upholding of precepts as the foundation” (they are called “practice” in the sense of actual performance — of genuinely carrying them out), and are obstructed by karmic hindrances.
You should repent diligently and genuinely

cultivate “ceasing evil and practicing good” and “taking the upholding of precepts as the foundation.” These two stages of practice are the foundation of learning Buddhism, and even more the foundation of single-mindedness without distraction. For this reason, “ceasing evil and practicing good” and “taking the upholding of precepts as the foundation” occupy the greater part of Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, and also a large portion of the Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha. In the Sutra of Amitābha Spoken by the Buddha, the Buddha said:
“One cannot, with few good roots, blessings, and conditions
(cannot, with few causes and conditions of good roots and blessings)
, be born in that land.”
Hence Master Yinguang said:
“One who recites the Buddha's name must in every matter keep loyalty and reciprocity
(loyalty, serving others with one's whole heart; reciprocity, extending oneself to others)
, and in every thought guard against faults and errors
(faults, mistakes)
. Knowing a fault, one must correct it; seeing what is right, one must do it — only then does one accord with the Buddha. Such a person will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land.
If one is not so, then one runs counter to the Buddha and can hardly achieve any sympathetic response.
(Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou)
In order to help reciters of the Buddha's name lay this foundation,
in the
Pure Practice division of the As-Taught Online Buddhist Academy

curriculum there are the two stages of “ceasing evil and practicing good” and “taking the upholding of precepts as the foundation”; I hope you will study them earnestly and carry them out in practice. Moreover, if obstacles and difficulties arise later in the practice of single-mindedness, they mostly stem from problems in “ceasing evil and practicing good” and “taking the upholding of precepts as the foundation,” and you should immediately make up the deficiency in a targeted way. Practice has shown that for a person of true faith and earnest vows, correct method, and unremitting persistence, single-mindedness without distraction is by no means unattainable.
Question: I have already attained single-mindedness without distraction; how should I practice from here on?

Answer: Single-mindedness without distraction is like mud settling so the water clears — it subdues afflictions. The next step is to remove the mud so the water is pure — to cut off afflictions. For this you should cultivate the samādhi of Buddha-recitation, and may refer to
A Detailed Explanation of the Record of Groping for the Elephant of the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi
and
The Essentials of Chan and Pure Land
. Of course, you may also investigate Chan (see
Awareness Chan
), and thereby achieve:
“With Chan and with the Pure Land, you are like a tiger with horns — in this life a teacher of people, in the next life a Buddha or patriarch.”
(Master Yongming's Fourfold Analysis)
Conviction has a decisive influence on whether one succeeds; it admits not the slightest timidity or hesitation. Let me illustrate with the case that “good or poor results depend on conviction”:

American psychologists believe that any student can learn any subject well. On this basis they reached the conclusion that “there are no students who cannot learn well, only teachers who cannot teach well.” To prove this, they gathered a class of students whose math grades were very poor and invited an excellent mathematics teacher to teach the class, while the psychologists followed the whole process. After several months, these students' math grades remained only in the forties or fifties. This result overturned the psychologists' earlier conclusion, and they had to re-analyze the cause. They found that these poor math students all held a firm conviction: mathematics was not only hard to learn but also dry and boring. With such a conviction, no matter how excellent the math teacher, their grades could not be raised. For this reason, the psychologists began to hypnotize these students for two hours every day; with their bodies and minds completely relaxed, they kept telling them that math was not only easy to learn but also very interesting, that they were all math geniuses, and so on. After a month of such psychological suggestion and guidance, these students' conviction about learning math completely turned around, and the earlier math teacher was invited back. A few months later, all of these students scored above ninety.

From this experiment we can see that conviction is a vital factor in whether one succeeds. For many children with poor grades, only by transforming their conviction can their learning potential be awakened and their academic performance raised.
Faith and success go hand in hand. Such maxims are everywhere. For example:
Success springs from confidence.
Confidence is the guarantee of success.
Resolve is strength; confidence is success.
Self-confidence brings success, self-strengthening brings talent, self-discipline brings growth.
The only secret of success: persevere to the last minute.

blocks.text: 3. As If Putting Out a Fire on One's Head

inline.s: Bodhisattva Samantabhadra's verse admonishing the assembly says:
“This day is already past, and life with it dwindles; like a fish in dwindling water, what
(this)
joy is there? O assembly: be diligent and vigorous, as if putting out a fire on your head! Think only of impermanence
(think only of the coming of death)
, and by no means be lax
(never indulge in careless pleasures)

[A fish in dwindling water] A fish in a pond whose water dries up day by day. [Be diligent and vigorous, as if putting out a fire on one's head] The fire on one's head is blazing fiercely and death is pressing in swiftly; one's recitation should be diligent and unremitting, hastening, urgently, to extinguish this fire of death and achieve single-mindedness before the confusion of death overtakes one. [Impermanence] The absence of permanence (all dharmas in the world arise and perish, flowing and shifting, not abiding for an instant); it also refers to death and to the ghost that seizes the soul. [By no means be lax] Never indulge in careless pleasures and waste your energy and time.

player! (Pay special attention to the poster at the end of the video.) And we, who must prevail over the emotional delusions of beginningless kalpas and escape the bitter sea of transmigration, should have even firmer resolve and even stronger willpower.
When you yearn for single-mindedness the way a drowning person yearns to draw fresh air, you will succeed!
The Buddha said:
Though
for one
lifetime you toil and suffer, in a brief instant afterwards you will be born in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, in bliss without limit.”
(The Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha)

, whose games are universally recognized as the most intense and of the highest standard in the world.
Practice constantly faces crossroads and the challenge of
material desires

flaring up at every moment. Your self-nature wants liberation while your physical body wants pleasure; which way you go depends on your wisdom in choosing the right path and your perseverance in holding to right practice — and intense self-motivation and unceasing self-strengthening are the prerequisites of success.

[Perseverance] Perseverance is keeping oneself in check with a firm and unyielding will: skill matures through diligence and is ruined through play; what should be done, do resolutely and do well; what should not be done, resolutely do not do, without hesitation. Perseverance is passion and striving toward a long-range goal, a lasting and enduring drive, your insistence on the future — day after day, turning your dream into reality. (Please watch
The Key to Success — Perseverance (video)

) [Self-motivation] Self-motivation refers to a psychological trait by which an individual, without needing external reward or punishment as an incentive, can work diligently on his own toward a set goal.
Practice has shown that investigative recitation and awareness recitation are effective methods for attaining single-mindedness. I suggest you practice down-to-earth according to
Investigative Recitation
or
Awareness Recitation
, and verify it through your own practice. Of course, you may also specialize in breathing recitation, which is likewise a very effective method; see
The Essentials of Breathing Recitation
Diligence without letup requires not only a strong will and scrupulous self-discipline, but also a scientific method. Please read repeatedly
Ten Thousand Hours of Deliberate Practice Makes a Genius

, and put it into practice. Comprehend it in practice, and use it to guide practice. Comprehending again and again, practicing again and again, make the principles and methods of the article concrete in your practice of recitation, and
single-mindedness without distraction will be the inevitable result!
Question: Does awareness recitation still require group practice?
Answer: Yes. If conditions permit, group practice once or twice a week is best.

In 1897, the psychologist Triplett observed that in bicycle racing, racing simultaneously with others produced better results than racing alone against the clock. Inspired by this phenomenon, he conducted an experiment in which children were asked to wind fishing line as fast as possible. The result showed that many children winding together wound faster than a single child winding alone. Later, more psychologists observed this phenomenon and called the improvement of efficiency in an individual's activity caused by the presence of others (playmates or onlookers) “social facilitation.”

Practicing together, besides the “social facilitation” described above, has an even more important benefit: you can encourage one another, exchange experiences, and often have examples to follow, with a good atmosphere and field to nourish you. This is the “group-practice effect.”
Group practice content: Dharma talks, Buddha-recitation, and exchange.
During group practice one should strictly observe: noble silence, the ten wholesome deeds, and compassion.
[Noble silence] Not speaking idle talk other than recitation. In The Western Direction Clearly Pointed Out, the Bodhisattva Jueming Miaoxing taught:
“Say one word less, recite the Buddha's name once more; beat the thoughts to death, and your Dharma body will come alive.”
(See
Commentary on The Western Direction Clearly Pointed Out

) [The ten wholesome deeds] Not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct; not lying, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not speaking frivolously; not being greedy, not being hateful, not being deluded.
